spec_choices.why: The designer fixed the table at 3, and the active-seat schedule (1,2,3,1,2,3,3,2,1,3,2,1) is written for three seats. Three is also the smallest table where a sealed-bid tie can void a lot and a majority can be split. A thoughtful player bluffs about the kept card, reads the others' bids and Church choices, and spends gold only where a majority can still be won.

spec_choices.what: Keep the simultaneous talk step as a poll broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The source requires it. It earns its place because players disagree about which colours should rise, and they can bluff about kept cards or try to steer bids.

spec_choices.what: Cards are named as text '<Colour> <value>' and 'Church'; the top of the deck is index 0 after the single setup shuffle
spec_choices.why: The source gives no card labels, and it needs a fixed hidden order with a top card.

spec_choices.what: Card values per colour are given as counts per value in parameters (two 1s, two 2s, one 3, one 4)
spec_choices.why: Every parameter must be a number.

spec_choices.what: Marks are stored as 'round:colour:direction:counts', with counts fixed when the mark is made
spec_choices.why: This lets scoring apply only the counting marks, in round order, by arithmetic, without working out again which card was kept each round.

spec_choices.what: Per-colour totals and final worths are explicit attributes computed at scoring
spec_choices.why: The majority rule needs these numbers stored as state so they can be compared across players.

spec_choices.what: The active player's choice of A or B is an ask to that seat alone
spec_choices.why: Only one player answers, and the answer is private.

simplifications.what: Scoring runs as conditional steps (when round == 12) at the end of round 12 rather than as a separate phase
simplifications.why: The step list is flat, so final scoring is gated by an arithmetic condition.

simplifications.what: A tie for most VP is shown as a shared win rather than a 'draw'
simplifications.why: The engine has no separate draw; players level at the top share the win, which is the same outcome in effect.

simplifications.what: Parts (a) and (b) of step 9 are one poll addressed to the active seat and, when it applies, the Church winner
simplifications.why: The source says they are answered at the same time; a seat that is both gets both questions in the same poll.

variation.original_summary: Biblios is a 2-4 player card game in two phases. In the Gift phase the active player splits drawn cards between a secret keep, a face-down auction pile and face-up cards for opponents. In the Auction phase players bid Gold cards for the auction pile. Church cards shift the VP dice on five colours, and the player with the highest total value in a colour wins that colour's die.

review.evidence: No simple policy dominates. Never bidding leaves a player with only gifted cards and loses majorities. Always overbidding drains Gold and leaves a player unable to compete later. Majority scoring means choices directly move VP.
Skill matters in splitting gifts and timing bids. But an 87-card shuffle, random theft when a player cannot pay, and a re-shuffled auction pile give luck a large share.
Card counting, reading opponents' secret keeps and steering dice give long-term room to improve. Weak players still win some colours.
Secret keeps and face-down auction cards hide state. Players infer rivals' colour totals and plan Gold across many rounds.
Scoring is sums and comparisons, with ties broken by card letters.

It is text-friendly with no board. But the 87-card deck, Gold-as-cards payment, overpaying, random theft, open-outcry auction re-runs, two-phase structure and letter tie-breaks exceed the step limits.

problems: The original's deck, payment-by-cards, theft and open-outcry auctions exceed platform complexity, and its many random steps let luck swamp skill.

The previous variation contradicted itself. Step 4 hid whether the kept card was a Church card, but step 9 announced 'a hidden Church card was used', which reveals both the card type and the user, since only the active player keeps a card.
The previous variation never said where a won Church card goes after it is used.
The previous variation called two Church adjustments simultaneous yet ordered, without saying whether the 2-8 limit is checked before or after the first adjustment.
A hidden Church choice that only some players are asked to make would itself leak information: being asked reveals that the kept card is a Church card.

changes.what: The original is reduced to a 36-card deck, abstract gold, one sealed bid per round, and the active player's keep-one-of-two choice standing in for the gift split. This is retained from the previous variation.
changes.why: It keeps the gift-and-auction identity within the step limits, with one shuffle at setup.
changes.fixes: The original's deck, payment-by-cards, theft and open-outcry auctions exceed platform complexity, and its many random steps let luck swamp skill.

changes.what: A kept Church card no longer changes worths during play. Its owner records a secret colour and direction in their hidden collection, applied only at scoring. Worths shown during play exclude these secret adjustments. Nothing is announced when a kept Church card is used.
changes.why: This keeps secrecy without contradiction, and makes reading which colour a rival secretly boosted part of the inference.
changes.fixes: The previous variation contradicted itself. Step 4 hid whether the kept card was a Church card, but step 9 announced 'a hidden Church card was used', which reveals both the card type and the user, since only the active player keeps a card.

changes.what: Every round the active player always gives a secret mark (a colour and +1 or -1), whatever they kept. The mark counts only if the kept card was a Church card.
changes.why: Being asked never reveals anything, because everyone sees the active player asked every round.
changes.fixes: A hidden Church choice that only some players are asked to make would itself leak information: being asked reveals that the kept card is a Church card.

changes.what: A won Church card is used at once in public (the winner names a colour and a direction, applied immediately) and is then discarded face-up. It never enters any collection.
changes.why: It gives the card a stated destination.
changes.fixes: The previous variation never said where a won Church card goes after it is used.

changes.what: During play only the public adjustment from a won Church card changes a worth, so at most one public adjustment happens per round. At scoring, the secret marks that count are applied one at a time in round order, starting from the final public worths. Each mark is checked against the limit using the worth as already changed by earlier marks; a mark that would take a worth below 2 or above 8 has no effect.
changes.why: This gives an exact, ordered clamping rule. For example, worth 7 with two +1 marks becomes 8, then the second mark has no effect.
changes.fixes: The previous variation called two Church adjustments simultaneous yet ordered, without saying whether the 2-8 limit is checked before or after the first adjustment.

keeps: The active player splits drawn cards between a secret keep and a card offered to everyone.
Gold-based auctions for the offered cards, with gold also worth points at the end.
Five colours whose majority holder scores that colour's die worth.
Church cards that move die worths up or down, now with a secret version.
Hidden collections that opponents must infer from what was offered and how players bid.

recommendation.reason: The three defects are rule-text problems with clean fixes, and the core of hidden keeps, sealed auctions, majority scoring and worth manipulation already fits the limits and rewards inference.

variation.name: Biblios: Sealed Scriptorium (revised)
variation.summary: Three scribes take turns drawing two cards, secretly keeping one and auctioning the other by sealed bid. Colour majorities score their die worth, which Church cards move in public when won at auction or in secret when kept.
variation.rules:
SETUP.
The deck has 36 cards.
- There are 30 colour cards: for each of the five colours (Red, Blue, Green, Yellow, Purple), one card each of values 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 and 4.
- There are 6 Church cards.
Shuffle the deck once. Its order is hidden from everyone.

Each player starts with 8 gold. Each colour has a public die worth, starting at 4. A public worth can never go below 2 or above 8.

Every player has two collections:
- A hidden collection, seen only by its owner. It holds the colour cards and Church cards they kept, and their secret marks.
- A public collection, seen by all. It holds the colour cards they won.
Gold totals and public die worths are public. The worths shown during play never include secret marks.

ROUNDS.
There are 12 rounds. The active player is seat 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 in rounds 1-6, and seat 3, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1 in rounds 7-12. Each round has these steps:

1. Announce the round number, the active player, all public die worths, all gold totals and all public collections.
2. Remove the top two cards of the deck. Show them privately to the active player only, as Card A (the top card) and Card B (the next card).
3. The active player privately chooses Keep A or Keep B.
4. The kept card goes into the active player's hidden collection. Nothing about it is announced. The other card is announced publicly as this round's lot.
5. Talk: every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages are not binding.
6. Sealed bid: all three players, including the active player, at the same time bid a whole number of gold from 0 up to the gold they hold.
7. Reveal all bids. If the highest bid is at least 1 and no other player bid the same amount, that player wins the lot and pays their bid to the bank (the gold leaves the game). Otherwise nobody pays and the lot is discarded face-up.
8. A won colour card goes into the winner's public collection.
9. Church and secret mark, answered at the same time:
   (a) The active player always privately names one colour and a direction (+1 or -1). This is recorded secretly in their hidden collection as this round's mark. It counts at scoring only if the card they kept this round is a Church card. Otherwise it is void. This question is asked every round, so being asked reveals nothing.
   (b) If the lot was a Church card and someone won it, the winner publicly names one colour and a direction (+1 or -1).
   If the active player is also the winner, they answer both parts.
10. If part (b) was answered, change that colour's public worth by the named direction. If this would take it below 2 or above 8, it has no effect. The won Church card is then discarded face-up. Secret marks change nothing now.
11. Every player gains 1 gold.
12. If this was round 12, go to scoring. Otherwise begin the next round.

SCORING.
1. Final worths. Start from each colour's public worth. Reveal all hidden collections. Take every mark that counts (made in a round where that player kept a Church card) and apply them one at a time in round order, earliest round first. Each mark changes its colour's worth by 1 in its direction, checked against the worth as already changed by earlier marks. A mark that would take a worth below 2 or above 8 has no effect.
2. Majorities. For each colour, add up the values of each player's cards of that colour, hidden and public together.
   - If one player has the strictly highest total and it is at least 1, they score VP equal to that colour's final worth.
   - If two or more players tie for the highest total (at least 1), each of them scores half the final worth, rounded down.
   - If no one has a card of that colour, nobody scores it.
   Church cards have no value at scoring.
3. Gold. Each player scores 1 VP for every full 5 gold they hold.
variation.objective: The player with the most VP after scoring wins. If two or more players tie for the most VP, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: The fixes make the rules consistent without losing the hidden layer. Since nobody knows whether a kept card was a Church card, and the mark is asked every round, players must infer secret worth shifts from behaviour: an unusually high bid for a colour, or talk pushing a colour. Public Church cards become contested lots because they move worths at once. Each player is active four times and sees two cards then; 12 cards are never seen, so colour totals must be estimated. Talk earns its place because all three compete for the same majorities and only one can win. A player might claim to be dropping a colour so rivals underbid, or urge two players to gang up on the leader. A player who simply believes such claims overpays or concedes a colour the speaker secretly holds, and loses. Simple policies all lose. Always bidding 0 leaves a player with four kept cards against rivals winning lots for 1 gold. Always bidding everything burns gold and gold VP early and leaves the player unable to contest the late lots. Always keeping Card A ignores the information the choice offers.

balanced.evidence:
Card economy: 36 cards, 12 rounds x 2 = 24 seen and 12 never seen. Each colour totals 1+1+2+2+3+4 = 13. Each player is active exactly 4 times (seat1: R1,4,9,12; seat2: R2,5,8,11; seat3: R3,6,7,10), so kept cards are equal by seat. The snake order also offsets seat 1's early lead. Gold: 8 start + 12 income = 20 maximum, which is at most 4 VP. The colour pool is about 5 x 4 = 20 VP, adjusted by Church cards, so majorities dominate but gold is a real alternative.

Thoughtless policies, judged by the winner rule:
(a) Always bid 0. Wins no lots. Holds 4 kept cards (about 9-10 colour value across 5 colours) and ends with 20 gold = 4 VP. The two sensible opponents split about 10 colour lots plus their own 4 kept cards each, for about 18 value each. The 0-bidder takes perhaps 0-1 majorities, roughly 4-8 VP total, against about 8-10 VP for each sensible player. It loses against sensible play. Against random bidders, who waste gold, it can sometimes win, which is acceptable. Not never-losing.
(b) Always bid all gold. R1 bids 8 vs 8/8: if anyone matches, there is a tie and no sale; otherwise it pays 8 and holds 1 gold. From R2 on it bids 1-2 and is outbid by anyone bidding 2-3. It ends with about 1-2 lots and 0-1 gold VP and loses to sensible play.
(c) Always keep A (or always B). This throws away the better card and is weakly worse. It is not dominant.
(d) Always bid 1. It wins only when both others bid 0. Once anyone wants the lot it loses it.

No bid is strictly better whatever the opponents do. The tie-cancels rule means a matching bid by an opponent denies the lot, so every bid can be beaten or blocked.

Payoff sketch for one lot worth swing V to the bidder: winning at price p nets V - p/5 VP. Losing nets 0, or -V if a rival leader takes it. There is a genuine trade-off between gold-VP and majority-VP.

Seat information: only the active player sees 2 cards. This rotates evenly. No seat advantage beyond the minor last-active position, which is held by seat 1 (R12) and offset by seat 1 never being active in R7-8. All three seats can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
Limits are fine: 12-13 steps per round (≤20); 4 choice steps (keep, talk, bid, church) (≤4); 16 attributes (≤20); 2 hidden elements (≤3); 0 random draws per round, with the shuffle done once at setup; 12 rounds (≤40). Engine fit: drawing from the deck uses the shared_deck_draw workaround. The majority comparisons at scoring use the player_attribute_compare / calc workarounds. This is costly but feasible. Talk is simultaneous, and with 3 players bidding against each other there is real disagreement (bluffing, ganging up on a leader), so talk is justified. The game is finite and scored by arithmetic. There are three defects.

1) Contradiction. Step 4 says others are not told whether the kept card is a Church card. Step 9 announces 'a hidden Church card was used' 'without saying who'. Only the active player can keep a card, so the announcement reveals both that the kept card was a Church card and who used it. A model cannot follow both rules.
2) A won Church card has no stated destination. Step 8 covers only colour cards, so it is unclear whether it goes to the public collection or is discarded after use.
3) Steps 9 and 10 call the active player's and the winner's adjustments simultaneous yet 'apply in order'. The rules do not say whether clamping at 2 or 8 is checked against the worth before or after the first adjustment. For example, worth 7 with two +1 choices: does the second have effect?

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance sources: the order of the 24 drawn cards and which 12 never appear. The active player's best-of-two pick reduces the variance of kept cards, and each seat gets 4 picks. Lots are public and contested equally. Rough split: about 30-35% chance (colour and value of the cards drawn when you are active, unseen cards making majorities uncertain), about 65-70% decisions.

If all players play well (keep the better card, bid up to the marginal majority value, use Church on colours they lead), the outcome still depends on bid sizing, on reading hidden collections, and on Church targeting. It is not settled by the deal alone.

Things to infer: (i) the kept card from the revealed lot and from the active player's later bids and Church choices; (ii) opponents' gold-versus-majority plans from public gold totals; (iii) bluffs in talk. Ways to act on them: sealed bids, deliberately matching a bid to cancel a leader's purchase, and Church adjustments. A reasoning player is clearly favoured over a random or thoughtless one, as the policy tests under balanced show.

required_changes: Remove the contradiction between steps 4 and 9. Either (a) drop 'nor whether it is a Church card' and 'without saying who', accepting that a hidden Church use reveals the active player, or (b) keep the secrecy by having kept Church cards adjust worths secretly, applied and revealed only at scoring. With (b), state that die worths shown during play exclude hidden adjustments.
State where a won Church card goes, for example: 'A won Church card is used in step 9 and then discarded face-up.'
Specify the clamping order for two adjustments: apply the active player's adjustment first, then check the auction winner's choice against the updated worth.

balanced.evidence:
ECONOMY. Each player has 8 gold plus 12 income, so 20 gold. Kept as gold, that is 4 VP, a rate of 0.2 VP per gold, paid only in full blocks of 5. Each colour holds value 1+1+2+2+3+4 = 13, and its worth starts at 4 (range 2 to 8). The colour pool is therefore about 20 VP of majorities, against about 4 VP each from hoarded gold. Twelve rounds use 24 of the 36 cards, so 12 colour or Church cards are never seen.

Each player plays 4 times as active player. Seat 1 is active in rounds 1, 4, 9 and 12. Seat 2 is active in rounds 2, 5, 8 and 11. Seat 3 is active in rounds 3, 6, 7 and 10. Each player therefore gets 4 private two-card choices: 4 hidden cards, plus 4 lots offered to the field.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule):
(1) Always bid 0. Against sensible play, opponents take lots at a price of 1 or 2 whenever they don't tie each other. The bid-0 player ends with 4 hidden cards and 20 gold (4 VP). Each opponent ends with 4 hidden cards, about 3 to 4 public cards and about 12 or more gold (2 VP). Opponents hold roughly twice the colour value and win most of the 5 majorities (about 4 VP each). The bid-0 player loses almost every game. Against random bidders, who waste gold, it sometimes wins but still loses majorities. Not unbeatable.
(2) Always bid all gold. It wins the round-1 lot for 8 unless tied, and then holds 1 gold per round. Opponents beat it with a bid of 2. It ends with about 0 gold (0 VP) and about 1 to 3 lots. It loses to sensible play.
(3) Always bid 1. Every sensible bid of 2 beats it. Against another bid-1 player, the tie rule voids the lot, so it wins nothing. It ends with about 20 gold (4 VP) and few cards, and loses.
(4) Always keep A (the top card). This throws away the active player's choice; the policy averages the same values but lands in the wrong colours. Against sensible play it is a mild handicap; it is not a dominant option.

No bid amount is strictly better whatever others do. The value of a lot depends on colour standings and on what opponents bid, and the tie rule punishes predictable bids. So no thoughtless policy never loses.

SEAT EDGE. Turn order snakes (1-2-3-1-2-3, then 3-2-1-3-2-1), so each seat gets 4 active turns. Seat 3's back-to-back turns in rounds 6 and 7, and seat 1's final turn in round 12, are small timing differences. Marks are applied in round order, but the order matters only at the 2 and 8 bounds. Bids are sealed and simultaneous, so there is no move-order edge in auctions. All players can realistically win.

There is no labelled payoff ordering to check, and this is not a cooperate-or-defect totals game, so the 'safe option' test does not apply. The 3-player auction has real conflict over each lot.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
SOURCES OF CHANCE:
- the deck order decides which 24 cards appear;
- the 12 unseen cards make the totals uncertain;
- the number of Churches drawn while active varies (about 4 of the 6 appear in expectation).

The active player always picks the better of 2 cards, which softens bad draws.

SOURCES OF SKILL:
- Inference: the public lot reveals what the active player passed up. A 4 offered as the lot suggests they kept a Church or a stronger card for a colour they want. Silent worth shifts at scoring must be guessed from what was not kept.
- Opponent modelling in sealed bids with a void-on-tie rule: bid one above the expected rival, or avoid matching.
- Planning gold against majorities: 5 gold = 1 VP, while a contested colour is worth up to 8.
- Deciding which colours to fight for, and secret marks that raise your own colours or lower rivals'.

The hidden-card and secret-mark uncertainty is bounded. Each colour's total of 13 is public knowledge, and public collections are announced each round, so careful tracking narrows the hidden holdings.

WITH ALL PLAYERS PLAYING WELL: the outcome is decided by auction prices, colour choices and reads of hidden holdings. A hidden type or deal alone does not decide it, so the random deal adds variety but can be overcome. I estimate chance at about 30 to 40% of the result. A careful bidder clearly beats the thoughtless policies shown under balanced.

design_flags_left: the built game has 21 steps per round, over the limit of 20
the built game has 5 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4

triage.reason: The rules are buildable on this platform. The attempts fail on two file-level bookkeeping problems, and the coder keeps fixing one while bringing back the other: talk/auction_colour fields shown blank, and a static `lot_list` attribute that no step ever changes.
triage.guidance:
Fix both problems in the same file.
(1) Blank fields. Give the per-player message attributes and the table's `auction_colour` hidden visibility (`none` on the table; hidden or bookkeeping on the player), or give them non-empty start values. Players should see the talk only through the talk/log output, and should see the auction card through the announcement or log text. Do not show them as empty state fields. Keep `auction_recipient` and the worths public, as the interface requires.
(2) `lot_list`. Do not keep a constant public list that nothing ever writes. Make it the deck: at setup, shuffle the 12 lots into a hidden draw list. Each round, remove the k-th lot from it (the deck recipe), so a step really changes it every round. Put the public list of all 12 lots in the game's rules or intro text, not in a mutable attribute. If you want a public record, add a `used_lots` attribute that a step appends to each round.
Check that every remaining attribute is both changed by a step that runs and is not shown blank. Keep all parameters as attributes, and use the single ending with `rank_by` = `you.vp * 1000 + you.gold`.

triage.reason: The failing test checks the length of `lot_list`. That attribute is not in the interface: it is the coder's own scratch value, emptied while shuffling the lots into `lots`, which holds the 11 lots not yet used after round 1 was dealt. Everything the interface does define came out as the rules say: seat 1 kept B1, G4 went to auction, both bids were 0, the auction card went back to seat 1, all gold stayed at 12 and the worths stayed at 3.
triage.guidance: Do not assert on internal attributes the interface does not name, such as `lot_list`, `lots`, `pick` or `current_lot`. To test that the lots are shuffled and each is used once, check only interface values and what can be seen in play. For example, play several rounds and check that the auction card announced each round comes from the 12-lot list. Or fix the lot order through `given` and check `auction_recipient`, gold and the worths. Keep the scenario's other expectations as they are: gold 12 for each seat and auction_recipient 1 after a 0-0 tie.

triage.reason: The game behaves as specified, yet a thoughtless policy dominates. Always taking the first option (keep the first card, bid 0) wins about 80-85% of matches, and always taking the last option (bid all your gold) almost always loses. Bidding is a losing proposition: the winner's gold goes straight to a rival, gold converts directly to VP, and tied or zero bids hand the card to the seller for free.
triage.guidance:
Rebalance the auction so that passing is not a dominant strategy. Options:
(a) Have the winning bid go to the bank instead of the active player, or only half of it to the active player, so buying is not a double swing to a rival.
(b) Make colour majorities worth clearly more than hoarded gold. Raise the worth range, for example start at 4 with a range of 2-8, or add a flat majority bonus. Weaken gold VP, for example 1 VP per 6 gold.
(c) On a tie, including both bidding 0, discard the auction card or give it to neither player, rather than rewarding the active player for an auction nobody contested.
(d) Optionally require a minimum bid of 1 to take the card, so a 0 bid is a clear pass.
Also address the seat imbalance (seat 3 wins 34 of 60 against random play). Consider letting each seat's last active turn fall at a comparable point, or giving later seats less starting gold. Re-check that neither 'always bid 0' nor 'always bid max' beats random play by a wide margin.

triage.reason: The game was built correctly and behaves as specified, but the design itself breaks the evaluation limits: 21 steps and 5 choice steps per round, against limits of 20 and 4. It is also unbalanced, with seat 2 winning about twice as often as seat 1 or seat 3 against random play.
triage.guidance:
Cut each round to at most 4 choice steps and well under 20 steps. The five choices now are keep, talk, bid, secret mark and church direction.

1. Remove one choice entirely. The simplest options:
   - Drop the secret mark (step 9a). A kept Church card could instead score a flat bonus, or simply be a blank that denies the lot.
   - Or fold the mark into the keep choice. The active player picks from options like 'Keep A', 'Keep B', with the colour and direction attached only when a Church card is kept. This also removes the void-mark bookkeeping and the round-ordered mark replay at scoring, which cost many steps.

2. Simplify the church-lot effect. For example, the winner of a Church lot chooses a colour, and the direction is always +1. This makes the step cheaper.

3. Keep the clamp, majority and gold scoring, but remove anything that needs per-round history replayed at the end.

4. Rebalance the seats. Seat 2 currently wins far more often than the others.
   - Use an active-player order that varies each seat's position more evenly. For example: 1,2,3,2,3,1,3,1,2,1,2,3.
   - Or make ties at the top of a bid resolve the same way for every seat.
   - Then re-check that no seat's win rate stands out.
